items_missed: No agenda statement. She asked permission ('I just wanna confirm a few things. Do you have a few moments to go over that?') but never set the roadmap or the timeframe — no 'I'll gather some details about your move, then walk you through pricing, takes about 10-15 minutes.' The customer never knew pricing was coming, which is why the rate landed cold at the end.

Packing services never probed or offered. The customer volunteered the opening himself — 'we're still kind of packing every doing right now, but it should all be ready by tomorrow' — on a move scheduled for the very next day. No question about whether he wanted packing help, no packing pricing, no acknowledgment of the time pressure.
No storage-stop question and no additional-stops question.
No additional-rooms probe — garage, storage unit, balcony, patio never asked at either apartment.

No moving-stressor question. Nothing resembling 'Is there anything you're particularly worried about with this move?' — so a next-day move with packing unfinished got no chance to surface the real concern.
Zip codes never confirmed at either address, only street and unit.

No what's-included list. Gas, truck, taxes, insurance, wrap, pads, bands, tools were never named. She said damage coverage is 'included in our hourly rate' but never told him what else the $206 buys, so the rate sounded like a bare hourly number.

Disassembly / reassembly never mentioned as included — a real miss on this specific job, because he described 'my bed set and my mattress... it's a king' and then flagged an uncertain dresser mirror: 'On the dresser there's a big near but I think it's connected. I, I'm not too sure if it could be disconnected.' That was a direct invitation to say the crew handles it at no extra charge, and it went unanswered.

No 'no hidden fees' pitch — no credit card fees, no transportation fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees never stated, on a call where the customer was clearly weighing price ('we'll think about that one').

Entire Clock section missing. No 'clock starts on-site when the contract opens,' no 2.5-hour minimum, no 15-minute prorated increments after the minimum, no sense-check. He was given $206/hour with no idea when the meter starts, what the floor is, or how partial hours bill.

No estimate. She gave an hourly rate and 'two movers 26 foot box truck' but never a typical time range for a 650 sq ft one-bedroom and never a dollar total — so the customer was asked to compare Saturday at $206 against Sunday at $192 with no idea whether the job was 3 hours or 6. Her own framing, 'so, it's a few bucks but,' understated a difference he had no way to size.

Variables never explained. Stairs at both ends (second floor with stairs at origin, third floor at destination), the king bed set, the 75-inch TV, the vanity set, and the 20-foot carries were all collected as data and never tied back to how they affect time or price.

Entire Save Your Ass section missing — the single biggest miss on this call. No 'prep before move day means a shorter move and a lower bill,' no consolidation examples, no 'take a carload,' no sense-check close. The customer had told her he was mid-packing with a next-day move and that box count was still moving ('maybe like ten at Max or like twelve'); that is the highest-leverage moment in the whole call for the prep speech and it was skipped entirely.

No booking attempt. When he said 'well, we'll yeah, we'll think about that, we'll think about that one,' she immediately conceded with 'what I can do is, I'll email you all this information.' She never asked for the business — no 'we have availability on both days, want me to go ahead and lock that in?' — on a move that was 24 hours out.
'No deposit required' never mentioned. On a price-hesitant customer one day from his move, the zero-risk close was available and unused.

No BOLDED-details framing for the confirmation email and no 'reply with any corrections.' She did tell him he could 'reply to the email and that'll we can put you on the books,' which is a booking channel, not a verification step.
Never asked 'any other questions before I let you go?' in the call — only the after-the-fact 'if you have any questions don't hesitate to reach out to us.' Business hours were never given.
Customer's name used only twice ('may I speak with Ethan?' and 'thanks Ethan') — short of the 3+ standard.
60 cents per pound baseline never mentioned alongside No Worries, so the coverage had no reference point.

Delivery stumbles: the date options got tangled ('could you do the six Sunday the sixth... Or I can do the Friday before' / 'Like today Friday' / 'Oh, you're right. No.'), the destination access was misread and corrected mid-sentence ('third floor with elevator access and then same thing, oh, stairs. Okay, sorry about that'), and the rate was delivered confusingly ('For Saturday is 206, and then Sunday so it's 206 an hour').
top_strength: The intake and the differentiator block were genuinely strong. Bri worked the quote form methodically and confirmed everything on file rather than assuming it — contact number, email, both addresses, both unit numbers, square footage and bedroom count at both ends, floor and access at both ends, and carry distance at both ends ('from where the movers can park the truck to the stairs you put twenty feet. Do you feel like that's accurate?'). She used a smart anchoring technique on box count instead of an open question: 'a typical box count for a move the size is about fifteen to 25 boxes you feel like you'd fall within that,' which got him to a real number. Her specialty-item probe was concrete and prompted the answers she needed — 'Anything that's heavy gym equipment? Safe. Large couch, heavy mattress' — and she followed up on the TV size rather than letting it sit. She then delivered all three differentiators proactively and accurately, unprompted, in one clean block: No Worries 'up to $2,000 per move to repair, replace or reimburse for accidental damages,' Meet Your Mover with the right reasoning ('helping ease attention or strangers arriving at your front door'), and the On-Time Guarantee ('if we can't make it in the time window that we arrange we immediately start discounting money of your final bill'). She also volunteered the cheaper option against her own Saturday rate — 'could you do the six Sunday the sixth and the rates are a bit cheaper on that day' — which is honest, customer-first framing.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: she gave a rate but never gave an estimate, so the customer had nothing to say yes to. After 'two movers 26 foot box truck' she needed to land the whole picture: 'Ethan, for a 650 square foot one-bedroom on the second floor going to a third floor, two movers and a truck typically runs 4 to 5 hours, so Saturday at $206 an hour comes to roughly $825 to $1,030, and Sunday at $192 comes to about $770 to $960. That includes the truck, gas, taxes, all the wrap and pads, and we disassemble and reassemble that king bed set for you — and there's no deposit, so locking in a day today costs you nothing. Want me to hold Sunday?' Right now the difference between the two days reads as 'a few bucks' when it is actually real money on a multi-hour job, and 'we'll think about it' was the predictable result of asking someone to compare two hourly rates with no total attached. Second priority, and nearly as valuable: he told her he was still packing for a move happening tomorrow and she said 'Okay, sounds good' and moved on. That is exactly where the Save Your Ass speech pays for itself — 'Since you're packing tonight, one thing that saves you real money: anything already in a box or consolidated when we walk in is time we don't spend. Empty the loose stuff out of drawers, get the kids' toys and the bathroom odds and ends into boxes, take the closet clothes and anything small in a carload yourself. Every 15 minutes you save is money off the final bill. Does that make sense?' She also skipped the entire clock explanation, which is a billing-dispute risk on any hourly quote — he does not know the clock starts on-site, that there is a 2.5-hour minimum, or that time bills in 15-minute increments after that. Add those four lines immediately after the rate, every time. Two smaller cleanups: get the destination access right before speaking it (she said elevator, then corrected to stairs mid-sentence, and third-floor stairs is a significant time variable she never priced), and answer the dresser-mirror question instead of saying 'Okay' — 'if it's attached, our crew will take it off and put it back on, that's included' is a free trust win she left on the table.
phone_presence_notes: Polite, brisk, and easy to talk to — 'No, you're fine' when he fumbled his unit number, 'Yes sir,' and a warm close that drew 'thank you so much. I appreciate your help' — but the warmth stayed at the level of courtesy rather than rapport, several stretches were pure data collection with 'Okay' as the only acknowledgment, and the tangled date and rate delivery cost her authority at the exact moment she was asking him to compare prices.
audio_review_reason: Two grading-relevant passages are unreliable in text: the destination access exchange ('third floor with elevator access and then same thing, oh, stairs' followed by the customer's garbled 'No, doesn't have space') leaves it genuinely unclear whether stairs or an elevator was established, and the rate delivery renders as 'For Saturday is 206, and then Sunday so it's 206 an hour' — audio is needed to confirm the customer actually heard two distinct rates and the correct access at the destination.
